Container.Name: github-runner
Container.Overview: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner, one instance per repository, running its own Docker daemon inside itself (Docker-in-Docker). Use it for a PRIVATE repository, where its minutes do not count against the account's Actions allowance — that is the usual reason to run one, since GitHub's standard hosted runners are already free for public repositories. DO NOT POINT IT AT A PUBLIC REPOSITORY: a job here is root in a privileged container, and on a public repository anyone can open a fork pull request. Nothing in this template names a repository or a host: set ACCESS_TOKEN, REPO_URL, RUNNER_NAME and LABELS per instance and the runner registers itself on start, appearing under the repository's Settings -> Actions -> Runners. Docker-in-Docker is what makes a workflow's services: container reachable at localhost the way it is on a GitHub-hosted runner, and it publishes nothing on the Unraid host, so several runners can each start a database on the same port without colliding. On Unraid it needs Privileged ON and START_DOCKER_SERVICE set to the exact string true. Read the START_DOCKER_SERVICE field before creating or converting this container: it carries the conversion checklist and one measured networking limit. One runner runs ONE job at a time; for concurrency add another instance with its own container Name, RUNNER_NAME and distinguishing label.
Container.Description: Self-hosted GitHub Actions runner (neutral template, one instance per repository) running its own Docker daemon inside itself. Set the PAT, repository URL, runner name and labels at creation. Privileged must stay ON and Network must stay Bridge. Private repositories only. The image tag is pinned; the runner binary self-updates regardless of it.

Config.Name: ACCESS_TOKEN
Config.Description: GitHub Personal Access Token used to mint short-lived runner registration tokens. Fine-grained, scoped to this ONE repository, with Administration: read and write (the permission that mints a registration token) — not a classic token with blanket repo scope. A token missing that permission does not fail any start-up validation: the container exits shortly after start, and the log shows an HTTP error from the registration-token request that looks much like the REPO_URL failure below. If REPO_URL is exactly right, suspect the token's permissions before its expiry. TRUST MODEL, and it is the reason this field matters more than it looks. This container is not a containment boundary and nothing in this template is one: a job on this runner is root in a privileged container, which is a short step from the host. So point this runner ONLY at a repository whose workflow code you control, and NOT at a public repository, where anyone can open a fork pull request. If you must accept outside contributions at all, go to Settings -> Actions -> General and, under the fork pull-request approval settings, choose Require approval for all external contributors; the default is narrower still, covering only first-time contributors new to GitHub, and is nowhere near enough for a privileged runner. WHAT A COMPROMISED JOB GETS: this PAT is repository ADMINISTRATION, so treat it as a compromised repository configuration and not merely a compromised runner — revoke it first, then audit webhooks, deploy keys and the runner list. TREAT IT AS EXPOSED TO YOUR WORKFLOWS: Mask hides it in this UI only, and Unraid stores it in plain text in the container's template on the flash drive. The image un-exports it before starting the runner, so it is NOT in a step's own environment — but job steps run as root in this container and can read it from /proc/1/environ, which is a snapshot taken at exec and unaffected by the un-export. As this template ships it, the PAT is NOT readable via docker inspect from a job: the in-container daemon did not create this container and has no record of it. That holds only while a job's docker client is talking to this runner's OWN daemon: it stops holding if the host's socket is mounted, or if the Docker data directory below is pointed at another daemon's store. The PAT is used at START to register and again at STOP to deregister, so rotating it while the container runs leaves that runner unable to deregister and a stale offline entry on the repository's runner page — rotate and restart while the old token still works, and note that sync-templates.py keeps timestamped whole-file backups, so the superseded value stays readable under templates-user/.template-sync-backups until you clear it. The image also accepts a short-lived RUNNER_TOKEN, or GitHub App credentials, instead of a PAT; neither is exposed here, but either removes the long-lived secret at rest if this runner's exposure ever justifies the extra manual step.

Config.Name: REPO_URL
Config.Description: Full URL of the repository this runner serves: https://github.com/OWNER/REPO — no .git suffix and no trailing path. Owner and repository are cut out of this string by field position, so a .git suffix becomes part of the repository name and 404s when the registration token is requested, while a trailing path is silently dropped there but passed to the runner configuration intact and fails at that later step instead. Either way the container exits shortly after start, and in neither case does the entrypoint stop at the point of failure — it carries on and dies when the runner binary starts with no valid configuration. Read the FIRST error in the container log, not the last. This template is repository-scoped, so this is always a repository URL.

Config.Name: RUNNER_NAME
Config.Description: The name this runner registers under. Name it for the REPOSITORY it serves and never for the machine it runs on — runner-REPO is the convention this template assumes, and the container Name above should match it so the Docker tab and the GitHub runner page agree. The name is printed in the job log of every workflow run (the Set up job step prints Runner name, Runner group name and Machine name), so a machine name written here is published to anyone who can read a run. Must be unique: the runner registers with --replace, so a second instance sharing a name does NOT error — it logs that a runner exists with the same name and then takes over the registration, which invalidates the FIRST instance's credentials and breaks it. The older runner does not compete for jobs; it simply stops working.

Config.Name: LABELS
Config.Description: THIS RUNNER EXECUTES ONE JOB AT A TIME; a second concurrent job needs a second container instance. Labels are the comma-separated names a workflow selects this runner by. The runner also adds self-hosted, Linux and X64 itself (unless registered with NO_DEFAULT_LABELS, which this template does not expose), and once registered those cannot be deleted from its page. So the shipped value adds nothing on its own, and that is fine while this is your ONLY runner: runs-on: self-hosted already reaches it. BEFORE ADDING A SECOND RUNNER, give each a distinguishing label — self-hosted,REPO — and target runs-on: [self-hosted, THAT-LABEL], or a job will pick whichever runner is free. The runner's full registered label set is not printed the way its name is, but the labels a job ASKS for are shown on the run, in a Requested labels line - that one comes from GitHub's side and shows in the web view of Set up job rather than in the downloaded log archive - and the runs-on: line naming them lives in the workflow file, which is world-readable on a public repository either way. Label by repository or by role, never by machine.

Config.Name: START_DOCKER_SERVICE
Config.Description: Runs a Docker daemon INSIDE this container, which is what makes a workflow's services: container reachable at localhost, and it is the reason this template exists in this shape. SET IT TO THE EXACT STRING true, AND TURN PRIVILEGED ON (Docker tab, Advanced View). Both are needed. The entrypoint string-compares this value and defaults it to false, so True, yes, 1 and an empty value all mean OFF — the opposite of EPHEMERAL below, which any non-empty value switches on. HOW TO TELL IT WORKED, AND WHY THE LOG WILL LIE TO YOU: the container log does show Starting docker service and then a Starting Docker line with a done marker, but that is NOT proof. service docker start launches dockerd through start-stop-daemon --background, which can only report whether the fork succeeded, and dockerd's own output goes to /var/log/docker.log INSIDE this container rather than to the container log. So the success line prints even when Privileged is off and the daemon died a second later. The real test is docker info: run it from a job step, or from this container's console alongside tail /var/log/docker.log. IF EITHER HALF OF THE PAIR IS MISSING THE CONTAINER STILL STARTS AND STILL REGISTERS. Registration happens before the daemon is started and nothing checks the result, so the runner reaches Listening for Jobs, shows Idle on the repository's runner page, and accepts jobs, and then every Docker step fails with a cannot-connect-to-the-Docker-daemon error. A healthy-looking runner whose Docker steps all fail means Privileged is off or this value is not exactly true. MEASURED LIMIT, and it is not specific to a conversion - check for it on a fresh install too: a container this daemon starts on a bridge network can have no return path out. On a runner attached to a CUSTOM Unraid network, its outbound SYN was forwarded and source-NATed correctly and no reply ever came back, so a build died claiming it could not resolve a package mirror when nothing was wrong with DNS. Workaround: docker build --network=host, which here means THIS container's namespace, not the Unraid host's, provided this container is on Bridge. A workflow's services: containers are unaffected either way. It was NOT reproduced on the plain bridge network this template ships, and not ruled out there either — so check for this rather than expect it. NOT A SECURITY BOUNDARY: removing the host socket bought networking, not safety. Privileged already puts a job one step from host root either way; see ACCESS_TOKEN for the trust model. DO NOT ALSO MOUNT THE HOST'S DOCKER SOCKET — it is the alternative to this, not a companion: mounted, containers are created on the HOST's daemon and their ports land in the HOST's namespace while the job's steps run in this container's, so localhost finds nothing. Note /var/run/docker.sock still EXISTS in a correctly configured container — that is the local daemon's OWN socket. To tell them apart run grep docker.sock /proc/self/mountinfo from a job step: nothing when the socket is local, a line when the host's is mounted. CONVERTING AN EXISTING SOCKET-MOUNTED RUNNER. Do step 0 FIRST, from the Unraid console: (0) run sync-templates.py, because stock Unraid does NOT merge template changes into a container that already exists, and START_DOCKER_SERVICE and the two path mappings below are not on its Edit page until that script has added them. Then open the Edit page and press Apply at the end: the script rewrites the container's SAVED TEMPLATE, and the container is rebuilt from that file by Apply, and equally by any container Update or force update, but never on its own. Check for update compares the image only, so a template edit never marks the container as update-ready. It will flag the docker-socket mapping, and the old work directory if you had filled one in, with a KEPT line; during THIS migration that is expected and means delete it in the UI, not put it back in the template. Then, on the container's Edit page in Advanced View, noting that steps 2 to 9 are edits to one form applied together at step 10 so only 1, 10 and 11 are truly sequential: (1) stop the container; (2) DELETE the /var/run/docker.sock path mapping; (3) set Network Type back to Bridge — the old design ran on Host, and no template merge will ever change that for you because Network is container-level; left on Host the service ports land in the Unraid host's namespace again and a second runner collides; (4) turn Privileged ON; (5) set this variable to true - the template merge will already have added it; (6) map the Docker data directory below; (7) set RUNNER_WORKDIR back to /tmp/runner/work and delete the old work-directory mapping, re-adding it below if you want it; (8) set the Repository to the tag this template pins, 2.336.0-ubuntu-noble, since an existing container keeps its own; (9) rename the container and RUNNER_NAME to something that does not identify the machine; (10) Apply — Unraid applies the page at once, so an abandoned edit changes nothing; (11) if the old runner is still listed under Settings -> Actions -> Runners, remove it - stopping the container normally deregisters it, so there is often nothing left to remove.

Config.Name: Docker data directory
Config.Description: MAP THIS. The container starts without it and Docker steps will even appear to work, which is what makes leaving it empty the expensive mistake. Unmapped, the in-container daemon keeps its whole store in this container's writable layer - and where Unraid's own Docker store uses overlay2 (docker-xfs.img, or a directory with an overlay2 backing filesystem) that layer IS overlayfs, which the kernel refuses as an overlay upperdir. The daemon then falls back down its driver list to vfs, which writes a FULL COPY of every image layer instead of sharing them. docker info still succeeds, so the check this template recommends elsewhere passes: the tell is the Storage Driver line reading vfs rather than overlay2 or a filesystem-native driver. Under that amplification a couple of CI runs fill whatever backs Unraid's Docker store: a fixed-size vDisk image fills and takes every other container's Docker down with it, and a directory-backed store eats the pool instead. Either way the store is shared with every other container, and CI images are large. Mapped, the store also survives a restart — measured, a later run reported the postgres image already up to date rather than pulling it again. Point it at a directory of this runner's own on an appdata share, for example /mnt/POOL/appdata/runner-REPO/docker with your own pool and repository substituted. Prefer a pool path over a user share, so the daemon's data root is not on the FUSE layer. RUNNERS ON ONE HOST MUST NEVER SHARE THIS, and never point it at the Unraid host's own Docker data-root to reuse the host's image cache: two daemons over one data directory corrupt it, and a job would be driving the host's image and container store rather than this runner's. Give each runner a directory named for the repository it serves. Where this was measured, with the directory mapped, the IN-CONTAINER daemon selected overlay2 over the mapped path; what your own pool yields was not tested, and docker info from a job step is what reports it.

Config.Name: RUNNER_SCOPE
Config.Description: Leave at repo; it is here for completeness, not as a choice. The image also accepts org and ent, but those modes ignore REPO_URL and read ORG_NAME / ENTERPRISE_NAME instead, and this template exposes neither. If you set one anyway, the image DOES print a clear line naming the missing variable (ORG_NAME required for org runners) — but that check runs its exit inside a subshell, so it cannot stop the container. What follows is an unlabelled but visible curl failure to mint a registration token, and then an opaque failure in config.sh. Read the FIRST message, not the last. An org-wide runner also accepts jobs from every repository in the org, so it is only as trustworthy as the least trustworthy workflow there — which matters more here than it would elsewhere, because this runner is privileged.

Config.Name: RUNNER_WORKDIR
Config.Description: Where the runner checks code out INSIDE this container. Leave as-is: it matches the container path of the optional work directory below, so mapping that one requires no change here. If you are converting an older runner, this field will still hold a host path left over from the socket model and sync-templates.py preserves applied values, so it will not be reset for you — set it back to /tmp/runner/work by hand. Unlike the host-socket model this replaced, the path does not have to correspond to anything on the host: the daemon runs inside this container and resolves a bind-mount source against THIS container's filesystem, so a job container, a Docker container action, or a service container that mounts the workspace all see the same files with no host mapping at all (measured — a container started from a job read the checkout, and wrote back into it, through a plain -v of this path). Unmapped, checkouts and build output accumulate in this container's writable layer, which the work directory below is how you avoid.

Config.Name: Work directory (optional)
Config.Description: OPTIONAL. Puts the runner's checkout on real storage instead of leaving it in this container's writable layer. Worth doing if this repository checks out anything large or its builds produce much output; skip it otherwise. The container path already matches RUNNER_WORKDIR above, so fill in a host path and nothing else needs to change — deliberately unlike the host-socket model, where the container path and the host path had to be the identical string. Give it a directory of this runner's own, for example /mnt/POOL/appdata/runner-REPO/work with your own pool and repository substituted, and NEVER share it between runners on one host or concurrent jobs corrupt each other's checkouts. Note that Unraid's /tmp is RAM-backed on the HOST; that has no bearing on this path, which is inside the container.

Config.Name: EPHEMERAL
Config.Description: OPTIONAL. Accepts exactly ONE job and then stops serving. ANY NON-EMPTY VALUE ENABLES IT, including the literal string false — to disable it, leave the field EMPTY. (Contrast START_DOCKER_SERVICE above, which needs the exact string true; the image does not treat these two the same way.) It also needs the container to come back afterwards, which neither this template nor Unraid configures: add --restart=unless-stopped under Extra Parameters, which is on this same Advanced View page below the variables, or the runner simply disappears after its first job. What does NOT carry over is the registration — GitHub removes an ephemeral runner's registration itself when the job ends, so the container's own deregistration at stop usually finds nothing to remove and logs a harmless failure. What DOES carry over: this container's filesystem when the same container restarts, any mapped work directory, and every image, volume and build-cache entry the job left in the Docker data directory. It is not a containment boundary — a job here is root in a privileged container either way — so it is not what makes untrusted or fork-pull-request code safe to run. Nothing here is.
